slides.body: Why packs exist: a loose object is one file per object, and each version of a file is a complete compressed copy.

In one sentence: a packfile stores many objects in one file and may store an object as a difference from a similar object, an index file beside it finds any object by ID, and none of this changes what an object is.

items: Saying "Git stores diffs" after seeing a pack listing. Root cause: a delta is a storage detail between two similar objects; every object still has its full content and its ID is computed from that content.
Blaming a commit for disk usage because its blob is the large entry. Root cause: the choice of base is arbitrary and can change at any repack.
Expecting packs to shrink model weights or compressed archives. Root cause: deltas need similar bytes.
Treating a missing .idx as lost data. Root cause: the pack index is derived from the pack and can be rebuilt with git index-pack.
Being surprised by loose objects after git gc. Root cause: every command that records content writes loose objects; consolidation happens later.

beats.text: You've told people for the whole course that Git stores snapshots, not diffs. A snapshot is the complete state of every tracked file at one moment, so every commit is a complete tree. If that's true, the whiteboard arithmetic looks right. And yet the repository on disk is small. Both statements have to be true at once, and this video shows how. Keep that whiteboard in mind. beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In the last two videos every object, every unit of Git's storage, was one zlib-compressed file under .git/objects, a loose object. That's how every object begins. It isn't how most objects are stored for long. Maintenance, Git's housekeeping, consolidates loose objects into a packfile, and inside a packfile an object may be stored as a difference from a similar object.

beats.text: Now precisely. Every command that records content writes loose objects. Maintenance later consolidates them into a pack. In this video that's git gc. The automatic strategies are the subject of Chapter 26 and of a later video. A pack is three files.
beats.tele: Now precisely. Every command that records content writes loose objects. Maintenance later consolidates them into a pack. In this video that's `git gc`. The automatic strategies are the subject of Chapter 26 and of a later video. A pack is three files.

beats.text: The .pack file has a 12-byte header: the signature PACK, a version, and the number of objects.
beats.tele: The `.pack` file has a 12-byte header: the signature `PACK`, a version, and the number of objects.

beats.text: Then one entry per object, and at the end a checksum of everything before it. An entry is a type, a size and zlib-compressed data. In the deltified form, the data is a list of copy and insert instructions against a base object, and the base is named by its offset in the same pack or by its ID.
beats.tele: Then one entry per object, and at the end a checksum of everything before it. An entry is a type, a size and zlib-compressed data. In the deltified form, the data is a list of copy and insert instructions against a base object, and the base is named by its offset in the same pack or by its ID.

beats.text: The .idx file is the pack index. It holds the object IDs in sorted order, a CRC32 and the pack offset for each, and a 256-entry table saying where the IDs with each first byte begin. A CRC32 is a small checksum, and an offset is a position in the file. Finding an object is a binary search in the index, then one read at the offset.
beats.tele: The `.idx` file is the pack index. It holds the object IDs in sorted order, a CRC32 and the pack offset for each, and a 256-entry table saying where the IDs with each first byte begin. A CRC32 is a small checksum, and an offset is a position in the file. Finding an object is a binary search in the index, then one read at the offset.

beats.text: The .rev file is the reverse map, from position in the pack to position in the index.
beats.tele: The `.rev` file is the reverse map, from position in the pack to position in the index.

beats.text: The manual states the principle in one line. I'll read it as written: "Conceptually there are only four object types: commit, tree, tag and blob. However to save space, an object could be stored as a 'delta' of another 'base' object."
beats.tele: The manual states the principle in one line. I'll read it as written: "Conceptually there are only four object types: commit, tree, tag and blob. However to save space, an object could be stored as a 'delta' of another 'base' object."

beats.text: How does Git choose what to compare? It's a heuristic, a rule of thumb. git pack-objects sorts the objects by type, size and name, compares each with its neighbours inside a window of ten, the --window option, and doesn't let a chain grow deeper than fifty, the --depth option.
beats.tele: How does Git choose what to compare? It's a heuristic, a rule of thumb. `git pack-objects` sorts the objects by type, size and name, compares each with its neighbours inside a window of ten, the `--window` option, and doesn't let a chain grow deeper than fifty, the `--depth` option.

beats.text: Three statements keep the two levels apart, and you should be able to say all three.
beats.tele: Three statements keep the two levels apart, and you should be able to say all three.

beats.text: First: a delta is between two objects chosen for similarity. It's not "the change a commit made". The base can be another version of the same file or a different file.
beats.tele: First: a delta is between two objects chosen for similarity. It's not "the change a commit made". The base can be another version of the same file or a different file.

beats.text: Second: IDs are computed from full content. So packing changes no ID, no tree and no commit, and git cat-file, git show and git checkout always deliver full content. On screen is the oldest version from today's demo, loose and then packed, with the same ID.
beats.tele: Second: IDs are computed from full content. So packing changes no ID, no tree and no commit, and `git cat-file`, `git show` and `git checkout` always deliver full content. On screen is the oldest version from today's demo, loose and then packed, with the same ID.

beats.text: Third: the choice of base, in the words of the git cat-file manual, "is arbitrary and is subject to change during a repack". So a size on disk says little about which commit "caused" it.

beats.text: When does this not help? Three limits. Deltas need similar bytes, so compressed archives and model weights gain nothing. Files above core.bigFileThreshold, 512 MiB by default, are stored without any attempt at deltas. And a clone transfers a pack, so everything reachable is downloaded however well it compresses.

Files above `core.bigFileThreshold`, 512 MiB by default, are stored without any attempt at deltas. And a clone transfers a pack, so everything reachable is downloaded however well it compresses.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy is a warehouse. It keeps one complete copy of a long contract and, for each earlier draft, a sheet of instructions: copy bytes 0 to 2,400 of the complete copy, insert these twelve bytes, copy the rest. You ask for a draft by its number and you always receive the complete draft.

beats.text: So keep two levels in your head. The object level is what Git promises: four types, full content, an ID computed from that content. The storage level is how the bytes happen to sit on disk today. The snapshot model lives at the first level. Deltas live at the second.

beats.text: Before I draw it, a quick quiz. Six versions of one file sit in a pack. Which one is kept whole: the oldest or the newest? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Six versions of one file. In the first row, a4e58256, stored whole: 1,372 bytes in the pack for an object of 16,789 bytes. Then 739088cd at depth 1, stored as a delta against it, 35 bytes in the pack. Then depth 2, 3, 4, and in the last row 0928d48c at depth 5.

beats.text: Now read the first row again. The newest version is the whole one, and the old versions are the deltas. If you said the oldest, that's the natural guess. It's the opposite of what "Git stores diffs" would suggest. To read the oldest version, Git reads the base and applies five deltas.

beats.text: Now the 🟡 command. git gc packs objects and refs, expires reflog entries by age, and deletes unreachable objects older than two weeks. A reflog is the local journal of a ref's past values, and an unreachable object is one that no name leads to. Preview what it could remove with git fsck --unreachable. Within the retention periods, nothing is lost.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Saying "Git stores diffs" after seeing a pack listing. Root cause: a delta is a storage detail between two similar objects; every object still has its full content and its ID is computed from that content.
beats.tele: Saying "Git stores diffs" after seeing a pack listing. Root cause: a delta is a storage detail between two similar objects; every object still has its full content and its ID is computed from that content.

beats.text: Blaming a commit for disk usage because its blob is the large entry. Root cause: the choice of base is arbitrary and can change at any repack.
beats.tele: Blaming a commit for disk usage because its blob is the large entry. Root cause: the choice of base is arbitrary and can change at any repack.

beats.text: Expecting packs to shrink model weights or compressed archives. Root cause: deltas need similar bytes.
beats.tele: Expecting packs to shrink model weights or compressed archives. Root cause: deltas need similar bytes.

beats.text: Treating a missing .idx as lost data. Root cause: the pack index is derived from the pack and can be rebuilt with git index-pack.
beats.tele: Treating a missing `.idx` as lost data. Root cause: the pack index is derived from the pack and can be rebuilt with `git index-pack`.

beats.text: Being surprised by loose objects after git gc. Root cause: every command that records content writes loose objects; consolidation happens later.
beats.tele: Being surprised by loose objects after `git gc`. Root cause: every command that records content writes loose objects; consolidation happens later.
